# Open Data Stack (odctl)

> Run an open data stack on your machine, with its services already connected, from one command.

# Home

# Open Data Stack (odctl)

**Run an open data stack on your machine, with its services already connected, from one command.**

odctl is a command-line tool that runs an open data stack on your machine with Docker Compose. You name the [profiles](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/how-it-works/#profiles) you want, such as `kafka-lite` or `airflow`, and odctl starts them together with the services they depend on.

A Compose file of your own is enough for one small project. [Why odctl](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/about/why-odctl/index.md) explains what odctl adds when several projects need different parts of the stack.

## Commands

Each command has its own section in the CLI reference, with its options and examples. The Example column links to a page that runs the command and shows its output, and [Getting Started](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/getting-started/index.md) runs them in order on one profile.

| Command                                                                  | Use it to                                                                    | Example                                                                                  |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [`odctl list`](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/cli/#odctl-list)         | See every profile and what it runs                                           | [Getting Started](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/getting-started/#start-a-profile)     |
| [`odctl explain`](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/cli/#odctl-explain)   | See a profile's services, images, ports and the profiles it depends on       | [Getting Started](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/getting-started/#start-a-profile)     |
| [`odctl ps`](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/cli/#odctl-ps)             | See the running containers, their health and their ports                     | [Getting Started](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/getting-started/#see-what-is-running) |
| [`odctl info`](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/cli/#odctl-info)         | Check the installed odctl version and whether Docker is reachable            | [Getting Started](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/getting-started/#see-what-is-running) |
| [`odctl init`](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/cli/#odctl-init)         | Copy the compose files and settings into `.odctl`, so you can edit them      | [Getting Started](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/getting-started/#create-a-workspace)  |
| [`odctl pull`](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/cli/#odctl-pull)         | Download a profile's images before you start it                              | [How It Works](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/how-it-works/#which-images-run)          |
| [`odctl up`](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/cli/#odctl-up)             | Start profiles and the profiles they depend on                               | [Getting Started](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/getting-started/#start-a-profile)     |
| [`odctl down`](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/cli/#odctl-down)         | Stop profiles and remove their containers                                    | [Getting Started](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/getting-started/#stop-a-profile)      |
| [`odctl logs`](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/cli/#odctl-logs)         | Read the logs of a profile's containers                                      | [Getting Started](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/getting-started/#see-what-is-running) |
| [`odctl restart`](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/cli/#odctl-restart)   | Restart a profile's containers and keep them                                 | [Getting Started](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/getting-started/#restart-a-profile)   |
| [`odctl recreate`](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/cli/#odctl-recreate) | Replace a profile's containers, to apply an edit to a compose file or `.env` | [How It Works](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/how-it-works/#examples)                  |

## What It Runs

| Area                                                                                                          | Technologies                                                                                                              |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [Messaging](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/profiles/messaging/index.md)                                     | Kafka (KRaft), Karapace schema registry, Kafka Connect, Kafka UI (kafbat)                                                 |
| [Stream and Batch Processing](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/profiles/stream-and-batch-processing/index.md) | Apache Flink, Apache Spark                                                                                                |
| [Analytics](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/profiles/analytics/index.md)                                     | ClickHouse, Trino, Metabase                                                                                               |
| [Orchestration](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/profiles/orchestration/index.md)                             | Apache Airflow, Temporal                                                                                                  |
| [MLOps](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/profiles/mlops/index.md)                                             | MLflow, Feast, Evidently                                                                                                  |
| [Metadata and Lineage](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/profiles/metadata-and-lineage/index.md)               | OpenMetadata, Marquez                                                                                                     |
| [Observability](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/profiles/observability/index.md)                             | grafana/otel-lgtm (OpenTelemetry Collector, Prometheus, Tempo, Loki, Grafana)                                             |
| [Storage and Catalog](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/profiles/storage-and-catalog/index.md)                 | PostgreSQL 18 with pgvector, pg_textsearch and PostGIS, SeaweedFS (S3), Iceberg REST catalog, Valkey Bundle, Apache Fluss |

Kafka Connect comes with a set of connectors, such as the Iceberg sink and the Debezium PostgreSQL source. [Kafka Connect](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/guides/kafka-connect/index.md) lists them all.

- [benchtop](https://github.com/jaehyeon-kim/benchtop): data engineering and machine learning projects, each run from a cold clone on odctl.

Blog posts about odctl and these projects are tagged [odctl](https://jaehyeon.me/tags/odctl/) on jaehyeon.me.
# Getting Started

# Getting Started

This page installs odctl, starts a first profile, runs each command on it and stops it. It needs no earlier page. The recording shows the main steps: install odctl, preview a profile, start it, list the containers and stop them.

## Requirements

- Docker Engine or Docker Desktop, running. Give Docker 8 to 16 GB of memory.
- Python 3.10 or later.

## Install

odctl is a command-line tool, so install it into its own environment with uv or pipx:

```bash
uv tool install odctl
# or
pipx install odctl
```

`pip install odctl` also works. `odctl --help` then lists the commands.

## Create a Workspace

Run this in the folder of your project:

```bash
odctl init
```

It prints `Workspace initialized!` with the path of the new folder. The command copies the compose files and their settings into `.odctl` in the current directory, and writes `.odctl/.env` with `TAG` set to the CLI version. odctl reads from `.odctl` whenever it exists, so you can edit any file there. [Workspace](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/how-it-works/#workspace) explains what changes with and without it, and how to customise it.

## Start a Profile

A [profile](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/how-it-works/#profiles) is a named group of services that start together. This lists every profile, with its parent stack and a description:

```bash
odctl list
```

Add `-d` to list each profile's services and host ports as well:

```bash
odctl list -d
```

This shows what one profile runs:

```bash
odctl explain kafka-lite
```

It prints a panel for `kafka-lite`: the parent stack `kafka`, the compose file, the profile it requires (`deps`), the containers `connect`, `kafka`, `kafka-ui` and `karapace` with their images, the host ports and how to reach each service. This shows the profiles `kafka-lite` would start, in order, without starting anything:

```bash
odctl up kafka-lite --dry-run
```

The dry run prints which compose files and profiles it would start:

Start it:

```bash
odctl up kafka-lite
```

odctl starts the profiles `kafka-lite` depends on first, then Kafka. It waits until the services are running, and healthy where they define a health check, then prints `All requested profiles successfully started!`. The [Messaging page](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/profiles/messaging/#kafka-lite) lists the same addresses as `odctl explain`.

## See What Is Running

This prints the installed CLI version and whether Docker is reachable:

```bash
odctl info
```

The output has two lines: `CLI Version:` with the version, and `Docker Daemon: ✅ Reachable`. This lists the containers of a profile, with their state, health and ports:

```bash
odctl ps kafka-lite
```

It prints a table with one row per container:

```text
┏━━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━┳━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┓
┃ Container ┃ Service  ┃ State   ┃ Health  ┃ Ports           ┃
┡━━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━╇━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━┩
│ connect   │ connect  │ running │ -       │ 8083 → 8083/tcp │
│ kafka     │ kafka    │ running │ -       │ 9092 → 9092/tcp │
│ kafka-ui  │ kafka-ui │ running │ -       │ 8086 → 8080/tcp │
│ karapace  │ karapace │ running │ healthy │ 8081 → 8081/tcp │
└───────────┴──────────┴─────────┴─────────┴─────────────────┘
```

A dash under Health means the service has no health check. This lists every container odctl manages, from every profile, including one-shot containers that have finished, such as `odctl-init-deps`:

```bash
odctl ps --all
```

This prints the last three log lines of one service, `connect`:

```bash
odctl logs kafka-lite -s connect -n 3
```

Each line starts with the service name, such as `connect | [2026-10-24 05:14:03,065] INFO [Worker clientId=connect-connect:8083, ...`. Leave out `-s connect` to read every service of the profile, and add `-f` to follow the logs until you press Ctrl+C. This prints the last two lines written between ten minutes and one second ago, each with a timestamp before it:

```bash
odctl logs kafka-lite -s connect --since 10m --until 1s -t -n 2
```

`--since` and `--until` each take a time such as `2026-10-24T05:00:00` or a duration before now such as `10m`.

## Restart a Profile

This restarts the profile's containers and keeps them, with their data:

```bash
odctl restart kafka-lite
```

It prints `Restarting containers...` and `Restart complete.` A restart does not apply an edit to a compose file or `.env`. `odctl recreate` replaces the containers to apply one, as [Apply a Change](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/how-it-works/#apply-a-change) explains with [examples](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/how-it-works/#examples). `odctl pull` downloads a profile's images before you start it, as [Which Images Run](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/how-it-works/#which-images-run) shows.

## Stop a Profile

This prints what `odctl down` would stop, without stopping anything:

```bash
odctl down kafka-lite --dry-run
```

This stops the profile and removes its containers:

```bash
odctl down kafka-lite
```

It prints `Teardown complete.` The data inside the containers goes with them, as [Where Data Lives](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/how-it-works/#where-data-lives) explains. It leaves the profiles that `kafka-lite` depends on in place, as [Which Containers a Command Touches](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/how-it-works/#which-containers-a-command-touches) explains. This stops every profile and also removes the named volumes, such as the shared jar volume `odctl-shared-deps`. It asks `Are you sure?` first, and stops only after you answer `y`:

```bash
odctl down --all --volumes
```

In a script, `--yes` answers the prompt:

```bash
odctl down --all --volumes --yes
```

## Code in the Guides

Every command and file in these pages is kept in the repository under [`docs/snippets`](https://github.com/jaehyeon-kim/odctl/tree/v1.3.0/docs/snippets), one folder per page, and the end-to-end tests run it on every release. A code block whose title names a file is a copy of that file, or of the section after the colon. The links on the published site point at the release that the docs describe.

## Use It with an AI Assistant

The docs site publishes [`llms.txt`](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/llms.txt), an index of these pages for AI assistants, and `llms-full.txt` with every page in one file. The repository also has an odctl skill in [`skills/odctl/SKILL.md`](https://github.com/jaehyeon-kim/odctl/blob/v1.3.0/skills/odctl/SKILL.md), generated from the profiles, which tells an assistant which profile to start and how to reach each service. For Claude Code, copy the `skills/odctl` folder into `~/.claude/skills/`.
# How It Works

# How It Works

This page explains how odctl chooses, starts and reaches its services, where their data lives and how to change them. It builds on [Getting Started](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/getting-started/index.md).

## Profiles

A profile is a named group of services that start together, such as `kafka-lite` or `airflow`. odctl uses Docker Compose profiles: each service in a compose file lists the profiles it belongs to. `registry.yml` lists every profile, the compose file it lives in and the profiles it depends on. A tool with a small and a clustered form has two profiles, `-lite` and `-full`, such as `kafka-lite` with one broker and `kafka-full` with three. `odctl list` prints every profile, and [Profiles](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/profiles/index.md) has a page for each one.

## What `odctl up` Does

Take `odctl up flink-lite` as an example. Flink keeps its tables in Iceberg, so it needs the Iceberg REST catalog. The catalog keeps its metadata in PostgreSQL and its files in SeaweedFS, an object store with an S3 API. All of them need the shared jars in `deps`.

odctl reads these links from `registry.yml` and starts the profiles from left to right:

1. `deps` copies connectors and jars into a shared Docker volume, creates the `odctl` network, and exits.
1. `postgres` and `storage` start, and odctl waits until they are healthy.
1. `catalog` starts once both are healthy.
1. `flink-lite` starts last.

This command prints the plan without starting anything:

```bash
odctl up flink-lite --dry-run
```

It lists each compose file with its profiles, from `compose-deps.yml` with `deps` to `compose-flink.yml` with `flink-lite`. Each [profile page](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/profiles/index.md) lists what its profile also starts.

### Dependencies and the Start Order

Each profile lists the profiles it needs under `depends_on` in `registry.yml`. odctl follows those lists from the profiles you name, one level at a time, until no new profile appears. It then sorts the result: `deps` first, `postgres` and `storage` next, `catalog` after them, and every other profile last, in alphabetical order.

The profiles are then grouped by compose file, in that order, and each file is started with one `docker compose up --wait`. That call returns once every service it started is running, and healthy where it has a health check, so a file starts only after the files before it are ready. `deps` is the exception: it starts attached, because its init container copies the jars and exits, and `--wait` treats an exiting container as a failure.

### Before Anything Starts

`odctl up` checks four things before it starts a container. The diagram shows them in order, and the list below explains each one:

1. **Docker is reachable.** If not, it stops.
1. **Every profile you name is in `registry.yml`.** An unknown name stops it, with the name in the error.
1. **Every service can be started.** A service that declares a profile owned by another compose file would never start, so odctl warns about it and carries on.
1. **odctl's own images exist for the tag.** It resolves `TAG` as compose does and asks the registry for each odctl image that is not already on your machine. If the registry says one is missing, odctl stops and names the tag, rather than leaving Docker to fail on one service. If the registry cannot be reached, it starts anyway, so a machine with no network can run images it pulled before.

### Which Containers a Command Touches

`down`, `ps`, `logs`, `restart` and `recreate` act only on the profiles you name, not on their dependencies. `odctl down flink-lite` stops Flink and leaves PostgreSQL, SeaweedFS and the catalog running for other profiles. odctl finds the containers by their compose labels: the project name starts with `odctl-`, and the service belongs to one of the named profiles.

There is one exception. When a profile depends on another profile in the same compose file, both are included, because compose refuses a command on a service whose dependency is left out. `odctl down --volumes` removes the shared `deps` volume and the `odctl` network only when no other profile has a container left.

## How You Reach a Service

Every service publishes its ports on the host at `127.0.0.1` only, so a browser or client on your machine uses `http://127.0.0.1:<port>`, and other machines on your network cannot reach them. This works the same on macOS, Linux and WSL2: Docker Desktop forwards the port to the host's `127.0.0.1`, and WSL2 forwards it to Windows' `localhost`. To open a port to your network, remove `127.0.0.1:` from its line in `.odctl/compose-*.yml` and run `odctl recreate <profile>`. Each profile page lists the ports.

Inside Docker, services reach each other by name on the `odctl` network, for example `http://catalog:8181` or `broker-1:19092` for Kafka. A container of your own reaches them the same way when it joins that network:

```bash
docker run --rm --network odctl curlimages/curl:8.17.0 -s http://catalog:8181/v1/config
```

With the `catalog` profile running, it prints the catalog's configuration as JSON, which starts with `{"defaults":`.

## Where Data Lives

Most services keep their data inside their containers. PostgreSQL, SeaweedFS, ClickHouse and Fluss's ZooKeeper are the exception: their images declare a data volume, so Docker gives each of these containers an unnamed volume, which a recreate passes on to the new container.

| Command                | Containers                                                           | Your data                                                                                 |
| ---------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `odctl restart`        | kept                                                                 | kept                                                                                      |
| `odctl recreate`       | replaced                                                             | lost, except in PostgreSQL, SeaweedFS, ClickHouse and ZooKeeper, which keep their volumes |
| `odctl down`           | removed                                                              | lost; the unnamed volumes stay on disk, unused                                            |
| `odctl down --volumes` | removed, with the unnamed volumes and the `odctl-shared-deps` volume | lost                                                                                      |

A database, a bucket, a topic or an Iceberg table therefore lasts until its profile is stopped, and every `odctl up` is a clean start. `odctl down --volumes` also frees the disk the unnamed volumes hold. The `odctl-shared-deps` volume holds only jars, so keeping it makes the next start faster.

Three profiles read their code from a SeaweedFS bucket, so uploading a file deploys it, and the upload lasts as long as the bucket does. The `storage` profile creates the buckets.

| Profile    | Prefix                         | What it holds          | How a change is picked up                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| ---------- | ------------------------------ | ---------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `airflow`  | `s3://airflow/dags`            | DAG files              | Airflow's S3 DAG bundle checks the prefix every 15 seconds (`refresh_interval` in `compose-orch.yml`), and the next parse of the file picks the change up                                                             |
| `feast`    | `s3://feast/repo`              | the feature repository | `feast-ui` and `feast-serve` list the prefix every 15 seconds (`x-feast-repo-sync` in `compose-mlops.yml`), copy it again when it changed, and restart Feast. An empty prefix gives the repository bundled with odctl |
| `metadata` | `s3://openmetadata/connectors` | connector modules      | `openmetadata-ingestion` lists the prefix every 15 seconds (`openmetadata/connector_sync.py`) and copies it again when it changed, with no restart, because each agent run imports the modules from disk              |

## Which Images Run

Most services run their project's official image, pinned to an exact version. odctl builds five images of its own and publishes them to `ghcr.io/jaehyeon-kim/odctl/`:

| Image      | Contents                                                                                                             |
| ---------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `deps`     | Connectors, jars and the Prometheus JMX agent, including the Iceberg REST catalog and the Kafka Connect Iceberg sink |
| `postgres` | PostgreSQL 18 with pgvector, pg_textsearch and PostGIS                                                               |
| `airflow`  | Airflow with the MLflow and Feast clients and the model runtimes                                                     |
| `mlflow`   | The MLflow server and model server with the model runtimes                                                           |
| `spark`    | Spark with the Python clients jobs use                                                                               |

These five are tagged with the CLI version through `TAG`. [Workspace](#workspace) explains how `TAG` is set with and without `odctl init`.

`odctl up` downloads the images it does not have. To download them first, for example before you go offline, pull a profile and the profiles it depends on:

```bash
odctl pull catalog
```

It prints `Fetching images for` each compose file, a `Pulled` line for each image and `All images pulled successfully!`. `odctl pull --all` pulls the images of every profile, which is many GB. To fetch newer images of the same tags as you start a profile, add `--pull`:

```bash
odctl up catalog --pull
```

## Workspace

odctl runs from one of two places: the files bundled with the CLI, or a workspace that `odctl init` copies them into.

### With and Without `odctl init`

|                                 | Without a workspace                                               | With a workspace                                                                     |
| ------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Files odctl reads               | the compose files and `registry.yml` inside the installed package | the copies in `.odctl` in the current directory                                      |
| Image tag of odctl's own images | the CLI version                                                   | the CLI version, written to `.odctl/.env` as `TAG`                                   |
| Your changes                    | none; the package is replaced on every upgrade                    | any file in `.odctl`                                                                 |
| After a CLI upgrade             | new files and images at once                                      | the old files and images, with a warning on every command until `odctl init --force` |

A `TAG` set in the shell overrides both. This shows the image the `postgres` profile would run with another tag, without changing the workspace:

```bash
TAG=1.1.0 odctl explain postgres | grep odctl/postgres
```

It prints the panel's line for the `postgres` container, with the image `ghcr.io/jaehyeon-kim/odctl/postgres:1.1.0`.

odctl looks for `.odctl` in the current directory. `--workspace PATH` uses the workspace folder at `PATH` instead, such as `../shared/.odctl`, so one workspace can serve several projects. It goes before the command:

```bash
odctl --workspace ./.odctl ps catalog
```

### Customise It

`odctl init` copies everything odctl runs into `.odctl`. It copies only files that are missing, so running it again keeps your edits.

| File                             | What to change                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| -------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `compose-*.yml`                  | Host ports, memory limits and environment variables of each service                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `registry.yml`                   | The profiles, their compose files and their dependencies                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `.env`                           | `TAG`, the time zone of the services that read it (`TZ`, `UTC` by default), extra Python packages for Airflow (`_AIRFLOW_PIP_DEPS`), the MLflow services (`_MLOPS_PIP_DEPS`), the OpenMetadata ingestion container (`_METADATA_PIP_DEPS`), whether OpenMetadata's AutoPilot creates default agents for a service added in its UI (`METADATA_AUTOPILOT`, off by default), and the model the MLflow model server serves (`MODEL_URI`) |
| `grafana/dashboards/`            | The Grafana dashboard for each service                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| `trino/rules.json`               | Trino's file-based access control                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `evidently/config.yaml`          | The Evidently server's settings                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `openmetadata/connector_sync.py` | How the ingestion container copies custom connectors from S3                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| `openmetadata/autopilot_init.py` | How the `openmetadata-init` service sets AutoPilot from `METADATA_AUTOPILOT`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

### Apply a Change

A restart keeps the container, so it does not apply an edited compose file or `.env`. Run `odctl recreate <profile>` to replace the profile's containers from their current definition. Add `--pull` to fetch the images again first:

```bash
odctl recreate catalog --pull
```

Recreating discards the data inside those containers, with the exceptions that [Where Data Lives](#where-data-lives) lists. `odctl restart <profile>` is enough for files a service reads when it starts, such as `trino/rules.json` and the Grafana dashboards.

### Examples

Each example edits the workspace, then applies the change. `sed -i.bak` works with both GNU and macOS `sed`, and keeps the original as a `.bak` file.

Give SeaweedFS 2 GB instead of 512 MB, for example when several projects share it. SeaweedFS is a Go program, and `GOMEMLIMIT` is a soft memory limit: as the memory the Go runtime manages nears it, the garbage collector runs more often and returns memory to the system sooner. It is three quarters of `mem_limit`, so change both:

```bash
sed -i.bak -e '/^  seaweed:/,/^  [a-z]/ s/mem_limit: 512m/mem_limit: 2g/' \
  -e '/^  seaweed:/,/^  [a-z]/ s/GOMEMLIMIT: 384MiB/GOMEMLIMIT: 1536MiB/' .odctl/compose-infra.yml
odctl recreate storage
docker inspect seaweed --format '{{.HostConfig.Memory}}'
```

The last command prints `2147483648`, which is 2 GB in bytes.

Publish Trino on port 8180 instead of 8080, when another program already uses 8080:

```bash
sed -i.bak 's/"127.0.0.1:8080:8080" # Trino/"127.0.0.1:8180:8080" # Trino/' .odctl/compose-analytics.yml
odctl recreate trino
docker port trino
```

The last command prints `8080/tcp -> 127.0.0.1:8180`.

Install extra Python packages in the Airflow container, for DAGs that import them:

```bash
sed -i.bak 's/^_AIRFLOW_PIP_DEPS=.*/_AIRFLOW_PIP_DEPS="dateparser==1.4.3"/' .odctl/.env
odctl recreate airflow
docker exec airflow python -c "import dateparser; print(dateparser.__version__)"
```

The last command prints `1.4.3`.

Install an extra Python package in the OpenMetadata ingestion container, for a custom connector that imports it:

```bash
sed -i.bak 's/^_METADATA_PIP_DEPS=.*/_METADATA_PIP_DEPS="dateparser==1.4.3"/' .odctl/.env
odctl recreate metadata
docker exec openmetadata-ingestion python -c "import dateparser; print(dateparser.__version__)"
```

The last command prints `1.4.3`.

Turn on OpenMetadata's AutoPilot, which creates and runs default agents for a service added in the OpenMetadata UI and is off by default. The `openmetadata-init` service applies the key each time `metadata` starts, and prints the result:

```bash
sed -i.bak 's/^METADATA_AUTOPILOT=.*/METADATA_AUTOPILOT="true"/' .odctl/.env
odctl recreate metadata
docker logs openmetadata-init 2>&1 | tail -1
```

The last command prints `AutoPilot active: true`.

Install an extra Python package in the MLflow containers, for a model that imports it:

```bash
sed -i.bak 's/^_MLOPS_PIP_DEPS=.*/_MLOPS_PIP_DEPS="tabulate==0.9.0"/' .odctl/.env
odctl recreate mlflow
docker exec mlflow-serve python -c "import tabulate; print(tabulate.__version__)"
```

The last command prints `0.9.0`. Each key installs its packages for its own containers:

- `_AIRFLOW_PIP_DEPS`: the Airflow containers.
- `_MLOPS_PIP_DEPS`: the `mlflow` and `mlflow-serve` containers, for example a library a served model needs to load.
- `_METADATA_PIP_DEPS`: the `openmetadata-ingestion` container, for example a library a custom connector imports.

All three install their packages from PyPI again in every new container: at the first `odctl up`, after `odctl recreate`, and after `odctl down` and `odctl up`. `odctl restart` keeps the container, so the packages stay. Each new container needs PyPI, and pinned versions (`transformers==5.20.2`) keep the installed packages the same.

Set the time zone of the services that read `TZ`, here the MLflow containers:

```bash
sed -i.bak 's/^TZ=.*/TZ=Australia\/Sydney/' .odctl/.env
odctl recreate mlflow
docker exec mlflow date +%Z
```

The last command prints `AEDT` from October to April and `AEST` for the rest of the year. PostgreSQL reads `TZ` only when it creates its data folder, and a recreate keeps that folder, so its time zone changes after `odctl down postgres` and `odctl up postgres`. `MODEL_URI` in `.env` sets the model `mlflow-serve` serves, as [MLflow Tracking and Model Serving](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/guides/mlflow/#serve-the-model) shows.

Create a bucket before its profile exists, for example for a project that has no profile. `seaweed-init` creates a fixed list of buckets, and `.odctl/seaweed/s3.json` gives the login `user` the `Admin` action, which creating a bucket needs. This runs boto3 in a container on the `odctl` network, where `seaweed:8333` resolves, and prints the buckets, which now include `desflow`:

```bash
docker run --rm -i --network odctl python:3.12-slim \
  sh -c 'pip install -q --root-user-action=ignore boto3==1.43.118 && python -' <<'PY'
import boto3
s3 = boto3.client("s3", endpoint_url="http://seaweed:8333", region_name="us-east-1",
                  aws_access_key_id="user", aws_secret_access_key="password")
s3.create_bucket(Bucket="desflow")
print(sorted(b["Name"] for b in s3.list_buckets()["Buckets"]))
PY
```

Two other ways exist. `weed shell` inside the `seaweed` container runs `s3.bucket.create -name desflow`, the command `seaweed-init` runs. Adding the name to `BUCKETS` in `.odctl/compose-infra.yml` creates it at every start of the `storage` profile. An upgrade needs `odctl init --force`, which removes that edit.

### Trino Access Rules

The shipped `trino/rules.json` grants every identity full table privileges and denies `analyst` schema ownership. Add your own table rules there for row filtering and column masking, then restart Trino.

### Start Again

`odctl init --force` deletes `.odctl` and copies the bundled files again, with `TAG` set to the current CLI version. Your edits are lost, so it asks for confirmation first. In a script, `--yes` answers the prompt:

```bash
odctl init --force --yes
```
# Profiles

# Profiles

A profile is what `odctl up` starts. These pages are generated from `registry.yml` and the compose files when the site is built.

## [Messaging](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/profiles/messaging/index.md)

| Profile                                                                         | Technology | Description                                                                               |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [`kafka-lite`](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/profiles/messaging/#kafka-lite) | Kafka      | Distributed event streaming and schema registry. Lite uses 1 Broker; Full uses 3 Brokers. |
| [`kafka-full`](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/profiles/messaging/#kafka-full) | Kafka      | Distributed event streaming and schema registry. Lite uses 1 Broker; Full uses 3 Brokers. |

## [Stream and Batch Processing](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/profiles/stream-and-batch-processing/index.md)

| Profile                                                                                           | Technology   | Description                                                                                      |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| [`flink-lite`](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/profiles/stream-and-batch-processing/#flink-lite) | Apache Flink | Stateful, real-time stream processing engine. Lite uses 1 TaskManager; Full uses 3 TaskManagers. |
| [`flink-full`](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/profiles/stream-and-batch-processing/#flink-full) | Apache Flink | Stateful, real-time stream processing engine. Lite uses 1 TaskManager; Full uses 3 TaskManagers. |
| [`spark-lite`](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/profiles/stream-and-batch-processing/#spark-lite) | Apache Spark | Distributed batch and micro-batch data processing. Lite uses 1 Worker; Full uses 3 Workers.      |
| [`spark-full`](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/profiles/stream-and-batch-processing/#spark-full) | Apache Spark | Distributed batch and micro-batch data processing. Lite uses 1 Worker; Full uses 3 Workers.      |

## Trino

Profiles: `trino`. Stack `analytics`, defined in `compose-analytics.yml`.

### trino

Depends on: `postgres`. `odctl up trino` also starts: `deps`, `postgres`.

```text
• Trino UI & JDBC connection (no password: no authenticator is
  configured, so any username is accepted):
  * External (host): http://127.0.0.1:8080
  * Internal (Docker): http://trino:8080
• Identities: `docker exec -it trino trino` connects as `trino`, the
  CLI default. Pass `--user user` for the stack-wide convention, or
  `--user analyst`, which trino/rules.json denies schema ownership
  while leaving every table privilege in place.
• Catalogs: postgres works with the trino profile alone. iceberg,
  kafka, clickhouse and valkey load without their backing services,
  so they appear in SHOW CATALOGS and then fail at query time unless
  catalog, storage, kafka-lite, ch-lite or valkey is also up.
```

| Service | Image               | Host:container ports | Memory limit |
| ------- | ------------------- | -------------------- | ------------ |
| `trino` | `trinodb/trino:484` | `8080:8080`          | `4g`         |

```text
• OpenMetadata UI & REST API (Credentials: admin@odctl.io / admin, or
  user@odctl.io / password, on a new database; a database from an
  earlier release keeps admin@open-data.local and user@open-data.local,
  both with the password admin):
  - External (host): http://127.0.0.1:8585
  - Internal (Docker): http://openmetadata-server:8585
• Ingestion Pipeline UI (Credentials: user / password):
  - External (host): http://127.0.0.1:8087
  - Internal (Docker): http://openmetadata-ingestion:8080
• Custom connectors: files in s3://openmetadata/connectors, checked every
  15 seconds and copied into the ingestion container when they change.
• AutoPilot (default agents for a service added in the UI) is off unless
  METADATA_AUTOPILOT="true" is set in .odctl/.env.
```

# MLOps

## MLflow

Profiles: `mlflow`. Stack `mlops`, defined in `compose-mlops.yml`.

### mlflow

Depends on: `postgres`, `storage`. `odctl up mlflow` also starts: `deps`, `postgres`, `storage`.

```text
• MLflow Tracking UI & Artifact Registry Server:
  * External (host): http://127.0.0.1:5004
  * Internal (Docker): http://mlflow:5000
• MLflow Model Scoring Server, idle until MODEL_URI in .env names a model;
  run `odctl up mlflow` again after setting it. It loads the model once,
  when it starts, so a new version behind the same alias needs
  `odctl restart mlflow`, and the server answers nothing for about 16 seconds:
  * External (host): http://127.0.0.1:5003/invocations
  * Internal (Docker): http://mlflow-serve:5003/invocations
• Liveness: http://127.0.0.1:5003/ping and http://127.0.0.1:5003/health
```

| Service        | Image                                             | Host:container ports | Memory limit |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | -------------------- | ------------ |
| `mlflow`       | `ghcr.io/jaehyeon-kim/odctl/mlflow:<CLI version>` | `5004:5000`          | `2500m`      |
| `mlflow-serve` | `ghcr.io/jaehyeon-kim/odctl/mlflow:<CLI version>` | `5003:5003`          | `1500m`      |

## Feast

### feast

Depends on: `catalog`, `valkey`. `odctl up feast` also starts: `catalog`, `deps`, `postgres`, `storage`, `valkey`.

```text
• Feast UI (registry browser, not data):
  * External (host): http://127.0.0.1:8890
  * Internal (Docker): http://feast-ui:8888
• Upload your feature repository to s3://feast/repo. The services check
  it every 15 seconds and restart Feast when it changes. Run
  `feast apply` from your own environment. odctl ships no definitions.
• Your environment needs: feast[duckdb,iceberg,redis,postgres]
• On an IcebergSource against catalog, pass warehouse="" and
  catalog_name="odctl". The REST client puts warehouse in the URL path,
  and Iceberg's REST fixture server serves the spec with no prefix.
• Online feature server for get_online_features:
  * External (host): http://127.0.0.1:6566
  * Internal (Docker): http://feast-serve:6566
• Liveness: http://127.0.0.1:6566/health
```

| Service       | Image                                    | Host:container ports | Memory limit |

# Orchestration

## Apache Airflow

Profiles: `airflow`. Stack `orch`, defined in `compose-orch.yml`.

### airflow

# Guides

# Produce and Consume with Kafka

The `kafka-lite` profile runs one Kafka broker in KRaft mode, the Karapace schema registry, a [Kafka Connect](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/guides/kafka-connect/index.md) worker and Kafka UI. KRaft mode means the brokers keep the cluster's metadata themselves, with no ZooKeeper. `kafka-full` runs three brokers with the same services beside them. The end-to-end tests run the commands below on every release.

This guide builds on [Getting Started](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/getting-started/index.md), which installs odctl and says where the code on this page comes from.

Start the profile:

```bash
odctl up kafka-lite
```

| Endpoint                                     | Address                                                                    |
| -------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Bootstrap servers from the host              | `127.0.0.1:9092` (`kafka-full` adds `127.0.0.1:9093` and `127.0.0.1:9094`) |
| Bootstrap servers inside the `odctl` network | `broker-1:19092`                                                           |
| Kafka UI                                     | `http://127.0.0.1:8086`                                                    |
| Schema registry (Karapace)                   | `http://127.0.0.1:8081`                                                    |
| Kafka Connect REST API                       | `http://127.0.0.1:8083`                                                    |

## Create a Topic

The Kafka command-line tools are in the broker container, which is `kafka` in `kafka-lite` and `kafka-1` in `kafka-full`. This creates the topic `demo` with one partition:

```bash
docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
  --create --topic demo --partitions 1 --replication-factor 1
```

The command prints `Created topic demo.`

## Produce and Consume

The producer writes five JSON records to `demo`, and the consumer reads them back from the start of the topic:

```bash
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do echo "{\"n\":$i}"; done | docker exec -i kafka \
  /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-producer.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 --topic demo

docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
  --topic demo --from-beginning --max-messages 5 --timeout-ms 60000
```

The consumer prints the five records, `{"n":1}` to `{"n":5}`, one per line, and then `Processed a total of 5 messages`. It reads through a consumer group, so its offsets are stored in the broker's `__consumer_offsets` topic.

Kafka UI at `http://127.0.0.1:8086` shows the topics, their messages, the consumer groups and the schemas in Karapace.

## Keep Messages Longer

The brokers delete old messages. A partition keeps data for one day or up to 500 MB, and a segment is deleted once either limit is passed. Both limits are set today in `.odctl/compose-kafka.yml`, where an edit can change them: `KAFKA_LOG_RETENTION_MS` is `86400000` and `KAFKA_LOG_RETENTION_BYTES` is `524288000`. A topic created without settings takes these values, which this command reads:

```bash
docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
  --describe --all --entity-type topics --entity-name demo | grep -E '^ *retention\.(ms|bytes)='
```

The output shows `retention.ms=86400000` and `retention.bytes=524288000`. To keep everything in one topic, set `retention.ms` and `retention.bytes` to `-1` when you create it. `-1` means no limit. Other topics keep the broker defaults. This creates the topic `history` with no limits and describes it:

```bash
docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
  --create --topic history --partitions 1 --replication-factor 1 \
  --config retention.ms=-1 --config retention.bytes=-1

docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-configs.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
  --describe --entity-type topics --entity-name history
```

The describe command lists the settings of that topic: `retention.ms=-1` and `retention.bytes=-1`. `retention.bytes` applies to each partition, so a topic with three partitions at 500 MB can hold 1.5 GB. To change an existing topic, use `kafka-configs.sh --alter --add-config` with the same two settings. If older messages are missing, see [Troubleshooting](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/troubleshooting/#older-messages-are-missing).

## From Another Container

Inside the [`odctl` network](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/how-it-works/#how-you-reach-a-service), clients reach the broker at `broker-1:19092`, and `kafka-full` adds `broker-2:19093` and `broker-3:19094`. Karapace is `http://karapace:8081` and Kafka UI is `http://kafka-ui:8080`.

## Runnable Example

Save this file as `example.sh` and run it with `bash example.sh` in the folder that holds your `.odctl` workspace. It starts `kafka-lite`, creates `demo` if it does not exist, writes five records and reads five back:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Starts kafka-lite, creates the topic demo, writes five records and reads them back.
set -euo pipefail

odctl up kafka-lite

docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
  --create --if-not-exists --topic demo --partitions 1 --replication-factor 1

for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do echo "{\"n\":$i}"; done | docker exec -i kafka \
  /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-producer.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 --topic demo

docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
  --topic demo --from-beginning --max-messages 5 --timeout-ms 60000
```

It prints `{"n":1}` to `{"n":5}` and `Processed a total of 5 messages`. When you run it again, it adds five more records and still reads the first five.

# Kafka Connect

Both Kafka profiles run one Kafka Connect worker, `connect`, beside the brokers. Kafka Connect runs connectors: a source connector writes records from another system into Kafka, and a sink connector writes records from Kafka into another system. The worker loads its connectors from the shared volume that the `deps` profile fills, and you manage them through its REST API. The end-to-end tests run the commands below on every release.

This guide builds on [Kafka](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/guides/kafka/index.md), which starts `kafka-lite` and reads a topic with the console consumer.

Start the profile:

```bash
odctl up kafka-lite
```

| Setting                             | Value                                  |
| ----------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| REST API from the host              | `http://127.0.0.1:8083`                |
| REST API inside the `odctl` network | `http://connect:8083`                  |
| Plugin folder                       | `/mnt/shared-deps/connect`             |
| Default converters                  | JSON with schemas, for keys and values |
| Offset flush interval               | 10 seconds                             |

The converters and the flush interval are set today in the `connect` service of `.odctl/compose-kafka.yml` (`offset.flush.interval.ms=10000`), where an edit can change them.

## Plugins

The `deps` image puts these connectors in the plugin folder: the Apache Iceberg sink, the Debezium PostgreSQL source, the ClickHouse sink, the Aiven JDBC connector, the Aiven S3 sink, the Redis connector and the MSK data generator. This lists the classes Connect has loaded:

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8083/connector-plugins
```

The reply is a JSON list with one entry per class. The tests check that it includes `org.apache.iceberg.connect.IcebergSinkConnector`, `io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector` and `com.clickhouse.kafka.connect.ClickHouseSinkConnector`. A plugin missing from the volume does not stop Connect from starting. It only leaves the class out of this list.

## Register a Connector

A connector is a name and a `config` object, posted to `/connectors`. The MSK data generator is a source connector that needs nothing but Kafka: it writes made-up records to a topic. Save this configuration as `demo-datagen.json`. It writes a record to the topic `customers` every half second, with an ISBN-10 number as its key, a first name and a number of visits from 1 to 10:

```json
{
  "name": "demo-datagen",
  "config": {
    "connector.class": "com.amazonaws.mskdatagen.GeneratorSourceConnector",
    "tasks.max": "1",
    "genkp.customers.with": "#{Code.isbn10}",
    "genv.customers.name.with": "#{Name.first_name}",
    "genv.customers.visits.with": "#{number.number_between '1','10'}",
    "global.throttle.ms": "500",
    "key.converter": "org.apache.kafka.connect.storage.StringConverter",
    "value.converter": "org.apache.kafka.connect.json.JsonConverter",
    "value.converter.schemas.enable": "false"
  }
}
```

The worker's default converters expect JSON with a schema envelope, so the connector sets its own: plain strings for keys, and JSON without a schema for values. Post the file from the folder that holds it:

```bash
curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  http://127.0.0.1:8083/connectors -d @demo-datagen.json
```

The reply repeats the configuration, with `"tasks":[]` and `"type":"source"`. The worker starts the task right after it answers.

## Read Its Records

The broker creates `customers` when the connector first writes to it, because automatic topic creation is on by default. This reads the first three records with their keys:

```bash
docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
  --topic customers --from-beginning --max-messages 3 --timeout-ms 60000 \
  --formatter-property print.key=true
```

Each line is a key, a tab and a value such as `{"name":"Patrina","visits":"3"}`. The names and numbers are random. The consumer ends with `Processed a total of 3 messages`.

## Check and Remove It

This reads the connector's status, then deletes it:

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8083/connectors/demo-datagen/status
curl -X DELETE http://127.0.0.1:8083/connectors/demo-datagen
```

The status shows `"state":"RUNNING"` for the connector and for task `0`. A failed task shows `FAILED` with its error. The worker's log has the rest:

```bash
docker logs --tail 40 connect
```

After the delete, the last lines of the log say that the worker stopped the task of `demo-datagen`. Kafka UI at `http://127.0.0.1:8086` lists the registered connectors under Kafka Connect, Connectors. [Ingest into Iceberg](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/guides/iceberg-ingestion/#kafka-connect-sink) registers a sink connector, the Iceberg sink.

## PostgreSQL for Debezium

The `postgres` profile runs PostgreSQL with `wal_level=logical`. Its init script creates the `cdc` schema and the `cdc_pub` publication for every table in that schema, so a Debezium source can read changes to tables you create in `cdc`. Start both profiles to use it:

```bash
odctl up postgres kafka-lite
```

## From Another Container

Inside the [`odctl` network](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/how-it-works/#how-you-reach-a-service), the REST API is `http://connect:8083`, and connectors reach the brokers at `broker-1:19092`, the catalog at `http://catalog:8181` and SeaweedFS at `http://seaweed:8333`.

## Runnable Example

Save this file as `example.sh` and run it with `bash example.sh` in the folder that holds your `.odctl` workspace. It holds the configuration above, so it needs no other file:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Starts kafka-lite, registers a data generator connector, reads three of its
# records, prints the connector's status and removes it.
set -euo pipefail

odctl up kafka-lite

# The REST API answers a little after the worker starts.
until curl -fs http://127.0.0.1:8083/connectors >/dev/null; do sleep 2; done

curl -s -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' http://127.0.0.1:8083/connectors -d @- <<'JSON'
{
  "name": "demo-datagen",
  "config": {
    "connector.class": "com.amazonaws.mskdatagen.GeneratorSourceConnector",
    "tasks.max": "1",
    "genkp.customers.with": "#{Code.isbn10}",
    "genv.customers.name.with": "#{Name.first_name}",
    "genv.customers.visits.with": "#{number.number_between '1','10'}",
    "global.throttle.ms": "500",
    "key.converter": "org.apache.kafka.connect.storage.StringConverter",
    "value.converter": "org.apache.kafka.connect.json.JsonConverter",
    "value.converter.schemas.enable": "false"
  }
}
JSON
echo

docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
  --topic customers --from-beginning --max-messages 3 --timeout-ms 60000 \
  --formatter-property print.key=true

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8083/connectors/demo-datagen/status
echo
curl -s -X DELETE http://127.0.0.1:8083/connectors/demo-datagen
```

It prints the reply to the registration, three records, `Processed a total of 3 messages` and the status with `"state":"RUNNING"`.

# Flink SQL: Kafka to PostgreSQL

The `flink-lite` profile runs a Flink JobManager, one TaskManager and the SQL Gateway. `flink-full` runs three TaskManagers. Flink's connector jars for Kafka, Avro with the schema registry, JDBC, Iceberg and HTTP come from the shared volume that the `deps` profile fills. The end-to-end tests run the commands below on every release.

This guide reads Avro records from Kafka through the Karapace schema registry and writes an aggregate to PostgreSQL over JDBC. It builds on [Kafka](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/guides/kafka/index.md), which starts `kafka-lite` and creates a topic. [Ingest into Iceberg](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/guides/iceberg-ingestion/index.md) shows Flink writing an Iceberg table, [Rolling Windows](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/guides/rolling-windows/index.md) computes features over several window sizes, and [Feast with Iceberg](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/guides/feast-iceberg/#push-features-from-flink-sql) sends rows to Feast over HTTP.

Follow the arrows from the TaskManager: it writes Avro records to the `orders` topic, reads them back and writes the totals to PostgreSQL.

Start both profiles:

```bash
odctl up flink-lite kafka-lite
```

`flink-lite` starts PostgreSQL itself, because it depends on the Iceberg catalog, which keeps its metadata there.

| Endpoint                                  | Address                         |
| ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| Flink UI and REST API from the host       | `http://127.0.0.1:8082`         |
| SQL Gateway REST API from the host        | `http://127.0.0.1:8084`         |
| Flink REST API inside the `odctl` network | `http://jobmanager:8081`        |
| SQL Gateway inside the `odctl` network    | `http://flink-sql-gateway:8083` |

## Create the Topic and the Target Table

This creates the Kafka topic `orders` and the PostgreSQL table `supplier_stats` that the job writes to:

```bash
docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
  --create --if-not-exists --topic orders --partitions 1 --replication-factor 1

docker exec postgres psql -U user -d odctl -c "
  CREATE TABLE supplier_stats (supplier TEXT PRIMARY KEY, orders BIGINT, total DOUBLE PRECISION);"
```

The commands print `Created topic orders.` and `CREATE TABLE`.

## Run the SQL

Open the SQL client in the JobManager container:

```bash
docker exec -it flink-jobmanager /opt/flink/bin/sql-client.sh
```

Run these statements in the client. They declare the topic and the PostgreSQL table as Flink tables, write three orders and sum them by supplier:

```sql
SET 'execution.runtime-mode' = 'batch';
SET 'table.dml-sync' = 'true';
CREATE TABLE orders (supplier STRING, price DOUBLE) WITH ('connector'='kafka','topic'='orders','properties.bootstrap.servers'='broker-1:19092','scan.startup.mode'='earliest-offset','scan.bounded.mode'='latest-offset','format'='avro-confluent','avro-confluent.url'='http://karapace:8081');
INSERT INTO orders VALUES ('a', 10.0), ('a', 5.0), ('b', 7.5);
CREATE TABLE stats (supplier STRING, orders BIGINT, total DOUBLE, PRIMARY KEY (supplier) NOT ENFORCED) WITH ('connector'='jdbc','url'='jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/odctl','table-name'='supplier_stats','username'='user','password'='password');
INSERT INTO stats SELECT supplier, COUNT(*), SUM(price) FROM orders GROUP BY supplier;
```

Each statement prints `[INFO] Execute statement succeeded.` or, for an `INSERT`, `[INFO] Complete execution of the SQL update statement.` The first `INSERT` writes three Avro records to Kafka and registers their schema in Karapace. The second reads them back, groups them by supplier and writes the result to PostgreSQL. `scan.bounded.mode` set to `latest-offset` makes the Kafka source stop at the end of the topic, so the batch job finishes. Leave it out and set `execution.runtime-mode` to `streaming` for a job that keeps running.

Right after Kafka starts, Karapace can answer its health check and still time out on a schema write for a short while. If the first `INSERT` fails on the schema registry, run it again.

## Check the Result

This reads the table the job wrote:

```bash
docker exec postgres psql -U user -d odctl -c "SELECT * FROM supplier_stats ORDER BY supplier"
```

Supplier `a` has 2 orders totalling 15, and supplier `b` has 1 order totalling 7.5:

```text
 supplier | orders | total
----------+--------+-------
 a        |      2 |    15
 b        |      1 |   7.5
(2 rows)
```

The Flink UI at `http://127.0.0.1:8082` shows the jobs the SQL client submitted.

The two `INSERT` statements run as two batch jobs, listed under Completed Jobs.

## From Another Container

Inside the [`odctl` network](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/how-it-works/#how-you-reach-a-service), Flink's REST API is `http://jobmanager:8081` and the SQL Gateway is `http://flink-sql-gateway:8083`. In Flink SQL, Kafka is `broker-1:19092`, Karapace is `http://karapace:8081` and PostgreSQL is `jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/odctl`.

## Runnable Example

Save this file as `example.sh` and run it with `bash example.sh` in the folder that holds your `.odctl` workspace. It runs the steps above with a topic and a table of its own for each run, so it can run again:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Starts flink-lite and kafka-lite, writes three Avro records to a Kafka topic
# with Flink SQL, sums them by supplier into PostgreSQL and prints the result.
# Each run uses its own topic and table names, so the file can run again.
set -euo pipefail

odctl up flink-lite kafka-lite

# Karapace answers its health check before it can store a schema, so wait
# until it accepts one.
until curl -fs -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/vnd.schemaregistry.v1+json' \
  -d '{"schema": "{\"type\": \"string\"}"}' http://127.0.0.1:8081/subjects/ready/versions >/dev/null; do
  sleep 5
done

run=$(date +%s)
docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
  --create --topic "orders-$run" --partitions 1 --replication-factor 1
docker exec postgres psql -U user -d odctl -c "
  CREATE TABLE supplier_stats_$run (supplier TEXT PRIMARY KEY, orders BIGINT, total DOUBLE PRECISION);"

docker exec -i flink-jobmanager /opt/flink/bin/sql-client.sh <<SQL | grep -E 'ERROR|Exception' || true
SET 'execution.runtime-mode' = 'batch';
SET 'table.dml-sync' = 'true';
CREATE TABLE orders (supplier STRING, price DOUBLE) WITH ('connector'='kafka','topic'='orders-$run','properties.bootstrap.servers'='broker-1:19092','scan.startup.mode'='earliest-offset','scan.bounded.mode'='latest-offset','format'='avro-confluent','avro-confluent.url'='http://karapace:8081');
INSERT INTO orders VALUES ('a', 10.0), ('a', 5.0), ('b', 7.5);
CREATE TABLE stats (supplier STRING, orders BIGINT, total DOUBLE, PRIMARY KEY (supplier) NOT ENFORCED) WITH ('connector'='jdbc','url'='jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/odctl','table-name'='supplier_stats_$run','username'='user','password'='password');
INSERT INTO stats SELECT supplier, COUNT(*), SUM(price) FROM orders GROUP BY supplier;
SQL

docker exec postgres psql -U user -d odctl -c "SELECT * FROM supplier_stats_$run ORDER BY supplier"
```

It prints the same two rows as Check the Result: `a` with 2 orders totalling 15, and `b` with 1 order totalling 7.5.

# Rolling Windows in Flink SQL

A feature such as the sum of a card's payments over the last 10 minutes, 1 hour and 1 day needs one rolling window for each size. A rolling window, or `OVER` window in SQL, aggregates the rows of a key that fall within a time range before each new row. Flink SQL refuses two different `OVER` windows in one streaming query, so this guide shows the two ways around it. The end-to-end tests run the SQL below on every release.

This guide builds on [Flink SQL](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/guides/flink-sql/index.md), which opens the SQL client and writes to PostgreSQL over JDBC. It needs only `flink-lite`, which starts PostgreSQL through the catalog:

```bash
odctl up flink-lite
```

The endpoints are those of [Flink SQL](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/guides/flink-sql/index.md). Open the SQL client:

```bash
docker exec -it flink-jobmanager /opt/flink/bin/sql-client.sh
```

## One Query Cannot Hold Two Windows

Flink's documentation says that for streaming queries the `OVER` windows of all aggregates in one `SELECT` must be identical ([Over aggregation](https://github.com/apache/flink/blob/release-2.2/docs/content/docs/dev/table/sql/queries/over-agg.md), Flink 2.2). These statements declare 20 generated payments, one a minute for two cards, and ask for a 10-minute and a 1-hour sum in one query:

```sql
SET 'execution.runtime-mode' = 'streaming';
CREATE TABLE payments (card BIGINT, amount DOUBLE, seq BIGINT, ts AS TO_TIMESTAMP_LTZ(seq * 60000, 3), WATERMARK FOR ts AS ts) WITH ('connector'='datagen','fields.seq.kind'='sequence','fields.seq.start'='1','fields.seq.end'='20','fields.card.min'='1','fields.card.max'='2','fields.amount.min'='1','fields.amount.max'='10');
SELECT card,
  SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY card ORDER BY ts RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '10' MINUTE PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS sum_10m,
  SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY card ORDER BY ts RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '1' HOUR PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS sum_1h
FROM payments;
```

The client prints `[ERROR] Could not execute SQL statement.` with this reason:

```text
org.apache.flink.table.api.TableException: Over Agg: Unsupported use of OVER windows. All aggregates must be computed on the same window. please re-check the over window statement.
```

## One Statement for Each Window Size

The first route is one statement for each window size, each writing its own table. This creates the two PostgreSQL tables:

```bash
docker exec postgres psql -U user -d odctl -c "
  CREATE TABLE card_sum_10m (card BIGINT, amount_sum DOUBLE PRECISION);
  CREATE TABLE card_sum_1h (card BIGINT, amount_sum DOUBLE PRECISION);"
```

Then run the two statements in a new SQL client session. The `sequence` field makes the source stop after 20 rows, and the event time `ts` makes each job write every row before it finishes. An `OVER` window on `PROCTIME()` would lose the rows still waiting for their timer when a bounded source ends:

```sql
SET 'execution.runtime-mode' = 'streaming';
SET 'table.dml-sync' = 'true';
CREATE TABLE payments (card BIGINT, amount DOUBLE, seq BIGINT, ts AS TO_TIMESTAMP_LTZ(seq * 60000, 3), WATERMARK FOR ts AS ts) WITH ('connector'='datagen','fields.seq.kind'='sequence','fields.seq.start'='1','fields.seq.end'='20','fields.card.min'='1','fields.card.max'='2','fields.amount.min'='1','fields.amount.max'='10');
CREATE TABLE sum_10m (card BIGINT, amount_sum DOUBLE) WITH ('connector'='jdbc','url'='jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/odctl','table-name'='card_sum_10m','username'='user','password'='password');
CREATE TABLE sum_1h (card BIGINT, amount_sum DOUBLE) WITH ('connector'='jdbc','url'='jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/odctl','table-name'='card_sum_1h','username'='user','password'='password');
INSERT INTO sum_10m SELECT card, SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY card ORDER BY ts RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '10' MINUTE PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) FROM payments;
INSERT INTO sum_1h SELECT card, SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY card ORDER BY ts RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '1' HOUR PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) FROM payments;
```

Each `INSERT` prints `[INFO] Complete execution of the SQL update statement.` once its job ends. This counts the rows of both tables:

```bash
docker exec postgres psql -U user -d odctl -c "
  SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM card_sum_10m) AS rows_10m, (SELECT count(*) FROM card_sum_1h) AS rows_1h"
```

Each table holds 20 rows, one for each payment:

```text
 rows_10m | rows_1h
----------+---------
       20 |      20
(1 row)
```

The cost is one job for each window size, each reading the source again, and one table for each size that a reader has to join on the key. With four sizes that is four jobs.

## One Function for Every Size

The second route is one `KeyedProcessFunction` in the DataStream API, which keeps the events of the longest window in Flink state and computes every size from them. This sketch is not run by the end-to-end tests:

```python
from pyflink.common import Types
from pyflink.datastream.functions import KeyedProcessFunction, RuntimeContext
from pyflink.datastream.state import ListStateDescriptor

WINDOWS_MS = {"10m": 600_000, "1h": 3_600_000, "1d": 86_400_000, "7d": 604_800_000}


class RollingSums(KeyedProcessFunction):
    def open(self, runtime_context: RuntimeContext):
        # Every event of the longest window, for each key, kept in Flink state.
        self.events = runtime_context.get_list_state(
            ListStateDescriptor("events", Types.TUPLE([Types.LONG(), Types.DOUBLE()]))
        )

    def process_element(self, value, ctx):
        now = ctx.timestamp()
        kept = [(t, a) for t, a in self.events.get() if now - t <= WINDOWS_MS["7d"]]
        kept.append((now, value[1]))
        self.events.update(kept)
        yield value[0], {n: sum(a for t, a in kept if now - t <= ms) for n, ms in WINDOWS_MS.items()}
```

One job computes all sizes, but you write and test the code in Python or Java instead of SQL, and you manage the state, which grows with the events of the longest window for each key.

## From Another Container

Inside the [`odctl` network](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/how-it-works/#how-you-reach-a-service), the addresses are those of [Flink SQL](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/guides/flink-sql/#from-another-container): Flink's REST API is `http://jobmanager:8081` and PostgreSQL is `jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/odctl`.

## Runnable Example

Save this file as `example.sh` and run it with `bash example.sh` in the folder that holds your `.odctl` workspace. It runs the first route with tables of its own for each run, so it can run again:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Starts flink-lite, computes a 10-minute and a 1-hour rolling sum over 20
# generated payments, one Flink SQL statement for each window size, and prints
# how many rows each wrote to PostgreSQL. Each run uses its own table names.
set -euo pipefail

odctl up flink-lite

run=$(date +%s)
docker exec postgres psql -U user -d odctl -c "
  CREATE TABLE card_sum_10m_$run (card BIGINT, amount_sum DOUBLE PRECISION);
  CREATE TABLE card_sum_1h_$run (card BIGINT, amount_sum DOUBLE PRECISION);"

docker exec -i flink-jobmanager /opt/flink/bin/sql-client.sh <<SQL | grep -E 'ERROR|Exception' || true
SET 'execution.runtime-mode' = 'streaming';
SET 'table.dml-sync' = 'true';
CREATE TABLE payments (card BIGINT, amount DOUBLE, seq BIGINT, ts AS TO_TIMESTAMP_LTZ(seq * 60000, 3), WATERMARK FOR ts AS ts) WITH ('connector'='datagen','fields.seq.kind'='sequence','fields.seq.start'='1','fields.seq.end'='20','fields.card.min'='1','fields.card.max'='2','fields.amount.min'='1','fields.amount.max'='10');
CREATE TABLE sum_10m (card BIGINT, amount_sum DOUBLE) WITH ('connector'='jdbc','url'='jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/odctl','table-name'='card_sum_10m_$run','username'='user','password'='password');
CREATE TABLE sum_1h (card BIGINT, amount_sum DOUBLE) WITH ('connector'='jdbc','url'='jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/odctl','table-name'='card_sum_1h_$run','username'='user','password'='password');
INSERT INTO sum_10m SELECT card, SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY card ORDER BY ts RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '10' MINUTE PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) FROM payments;
INSERT INTO sum_1h SELECT card, SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY card ORDER BY ts RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL '1' HOUR PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) FROM payments;
SQL

docker exec postgres psql -U user -d odctl -c "
  SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM card_sum_10m_$run) AS rows_10m, (SELECT count(*) FROM card_sum_1h_$run) AS rows_1h"
```

It prints `rows_10m` and `rows_1h` as `20` and `20`.

# Fluss

Apache Fluss is a streaming storage for real-time analytics: it keeps tables that Flink writes and reads with low latency, either as logs or as tables with a primary key. The `fluss` profile runs a coordinator server, one tablet server and the ZooKeeper they register in. Flink reads and writes Fluss tables through the Fluss catalog, whose client jar comes from the shared volume that the `deps` profile fills. The end-to-end tests run the commands below on every release.

This guide builds on [Flink SQL](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/guides/flink-sql/index.md), which opens the SQL client. Start both profiles:

```bash
odctl up fluss flink-lite
```

| Endpoint                                 | Address                  |
| ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| Coordinator inside the `odctl` network   | `fluss-coordinator:9123` |
| Tablet server inside the `odctl` network | `fluss-tablet-1:9123`    |

The coordinator is also published on `127.0.0.1:9123` and the tablet server on `127.0.0.1:9124`. Both advertise their container names, which resolve only inside the `odctl` network, so run Fluss clients in a container, such as Flink.

## Check the Cluster Formed

The servers register in ZooKeeper once they are up. This lists the tablet servers and reads the active coordinator:

```bash
docker exec fluss-zookeeper zkCli.sh -server localhost:2181 ls /fluss/tabletservers/ids
docker exec fluss-zookeeper zkCli.sh -server localhost:2181 get /fluss/coordinators/active
```

Among the ZooKeeper client's log lines, the first command prints `[0]`, the id of the one tablet server. The second prints a JSON object whose `listeners` include `CLIENT://fluss-coordinator:9123`.

## Write and Read a Table with Flink SQL

Open the SQL client in the JobManager container:

```bash
docker exec -it flink-jobmanager /opt/flink/bin/sql-client.sh
```

Run these statements in the client. They register the Fluss catalog, create a table with a primary key, write three rows and read them back:

```sql
SET 'execution.runtime-mode' = 'batch';
SET 'table.dml-sync' = 'true';
SET 'sql-client.execution.result-mode' = 'tableau';
CREATE CATALOG fluss_catalog WITH ('type' = 'fluss', 'bootstrap.servers' = 'fluss-coordinator:9123');
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS fluss_catalog.demo;
CREATE TABLE fluss_catalog.demo.t (id BIGINT, name STRING, PRIMARY KEY (id) NOT ENFORCED);
INSERT INTO fluss_catalog.demo.t VALUES (1, 'a'), (2, 'b'), (3, 'c');
SELECT * FROM fluss_catalog.demo.t LIMIT 10;
```

The `SELECT` returns the three rows:

```text
| id | name |
+----+------+
|  1 |    a |
|  2 |    b |
|  3 |    c |
+----+------+
```

Fluss keeps its data inside its containers, so [`odctl down` removes it](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/how-it-works/#where-data-lives).

The Flink UI lists the two jobs:

## From Another Container

Inside the [`odctl` network](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/how-it-works/#how-you-reach-a-service), set a Fluss client's bootstrap servers to `fluss-coordinator:9123`.

## Runnable Example

Save this file as `example.sh` and run it with `bash example.sh` in the folder that holds your `.odctl` workspace. It waits until the tablet server has registered, then runs the SQL above with a table of its own for each run:

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Starts fluss and flink-lite, then writes three rows to a Fluss table with
# Flink SQL and reads them back. Each run uses its own table name.
set -euo pipefail

odctl up fluss flink-lite

# The tablet server registers in ZooKeeper a few seconds after it starts.
until docker exec fluss-zookeeper zkCli.sh -server localhost:2181 ls /fluss/tabletservers/ids 2>/dev/null | grep '^\[0' >/dev/null; do
  sleep 2
done

run=$(date +%s)
docker exec -i flink-jobmanager /opt/flink/bin/sql-client.sh <<SQL | grep -E '^[|+]|ERROR'
SET 'execution.runtime-mode' = 'batch';
SET 'table.dml-sync' = 'true';
SET 'sql-client.execution.result-mode' = 'tableau';
CREATE CATALOG fluss_catalog WITH ('type' = 'fluss', 'bootstrap.servers' = 'fluss-coordinator:9123');
CREATE DATABASE IF NOT EXISTS fluss_catalog.demo;
CREATE TABLE fluss_catalog.demo.t_$run (id BIGINT, name STRING, PRIMARY KEY (id) NOT ENFORCED);
INSERT INTO fluss_catalog.demo.t_$run VALUES (1, 'a'), (2, 'b'), (3, 'c');
SELECT * FROM fluss_catalog.demo.t_$run LIMIT 10;
SQL
```

It prints the same three rows as the `SELECT` above.

# Ingest into Iceberg

Kafka Connect, Flink and Spark all write Iceberg tables through the same REST catalog, `http://catalog:8181`, with the files on SeaweedFS under `s3://warehouse`. SeaweedFS is an object store with an S3 API, which odctl's `storage` profile runs. The end-to-end tests run the commands below on every release.

This guide builds on [Kafka Connect](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/guides/kafka-connect/index.md), which registers a connector, and [Flink SQL](https://jaehyeon.me/odctl/latest/guides/flink-sql/index.md), which runs statements in the SQL client.

`kafka-lite` does not start the catalog, so start both:

```bash
odctl up kafka-lite catalog
```

| Endpoint                                    | Address                 |
| ------------------------------------------- | ----------------------- |
| Catalog REST API from the host              | `http://127.0.0.1:8181` |
| Catalog REST API inside the `odctl` network | `http://catalog:8181`   |
| SeaweedFS S3 API from the host              | `http://127.0.0.1:8333` |
| SeaweedFS S3 API inside the `odctl` network | `http://seaweed:8333`   |
| SeaweedFS file browser                      | `http://127.0.0.1:8889` |

## Kafka Connect Sink

The Iceberg sink in Kafka Connect reads a topic and commits its records to an Iceberg table through the catalog. Look at the sink in the middle: it writes data files to SeaweedFS and commits each batch through the catalog, which keeps its tables in PostgreSQL.

The sink writes to a table that exists. This creates the namespace `demo` and the table `kc` through the catalog's REST API:

```bash
api=http://127.0.0.1:8181/v1/namespaces
curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"namespace":["demo"]}' "$api"
curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"kc","schema":{"type":"struct","schema-id":0,"fields":[{"id":1,"name":"id","required":false,"type":"long"},{"id":2,"name":"name","required":false,"type":"string"}]}}' \
  "$api/demo/tables"
```

Each call answers with the namespace or the table's metadata as JSON. The sink also needs its topic and a control topic, where its tasks agree on each commit. This creates both and writes five JSON records:

```bash
for topic in demo-iceberg control-iceberg; do
  docker exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 \
    --create --if-not-exists --topic "$topic" --partitions 1 --replication-factor 1
done
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do echo "{\"id\":$i,\"name\":\"n$i\"}"; done | docker exec -i kafka \
  /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-console-producer.sh --bootstrap-server broker-1:19092 --topic demo-iceberg
```

Save the sink's configuration as `demo-iceberg.json`. It reads plain JSON, so it sets `"value.converter.schemas.enable": "false"` instead of the worker's default:

```json
{
  "name": "demo-iceberg",
  "config": {
    "connector.class": "org.apache.iceberg.connect.IcebergSinkConnector",
    "tasks.max": "1",
    "topics": "demo-iceberg",
    "value.converter": "org.apache.kafka.connect.json.JsonConverter",
    "value.converter.schemas.enable": "false",
    "key.converter": "org.apache.kafka.connect.storage.StringConverter",
    "iceberg.tables": "demo.kc",
    "iceberg.control.commit.interval-ms": "10000",
```
